title: We Asked 8 Sommeliers: Which Sancerre Is Actually Worth the Price?
summary:

Decades of commercialization and the pursuit of mass-market appeal have flattened many expressions of the grape and in the process disillusioned wine professionals about its potential. Through it all, however, one region has stayed steadfast in its commitment to Sauvignon Blanc in its purest form and remained a beloved beacon for wine lovers everywhere: Sancerre.

content:
There is perhaps no white grape in the world of wine as beloved by drinkers or as maligned by sommeliers as Sauvignon Blanc. Decades of commercialization and the pursuit of mass-market appeal have flattened many expressions of the grape and in the process disillusioned wine professionals about its potential. Through it all, however, one region has stayed steadfast in its commitment to Sauvignon Blanc in its purest form and remained a beloved beacon for wine lovers everywhere: Sancerre.

Located on the eastern edge of the Loire Valley, Sancerre is a region dedicated foremost to the cultivation of Sauvignon Blanc, which accounts for 80 percent of the appellation’s plantings. The region’s distinctive terroir — a mix of Kimmeridgian marl, flinty silex, and stony, limestone-rich soils — gives rise to some of the world’s most nuanced and age-worthy expressions of the grape. The result is a wine defined by its bright acidity, rooted in notes of lemon zest, wet stone, and fresh-cut grass.

Over the years, Sancerre’s enduring popularity has steadily driven the prices up — but not every bottle that dons a $50-plus price tag delivers on quality. Increased interest in the region has challenged sommeliers to dig deeper to find bottles that truly deliver on taste. That’s why we asked eight wine professionals to share which bottles are really worth the elevated cost that comes with the “Sancerre” label.

Sancerre wines that are actually worth the price, according to sommeliers:

  • Vincent Gaudry ‘Le Tournebride’ Sancerre 2024
  • Lucien Crochet ‘La Croix du Roy’ Sancerre 2024
  • Domaine Vacheron Guigne-Chèvres Sancerre
  • Vincent Gaudry ‘Mélodie de Vieilles Vignes’
  • Domaine B. Millet Sancerre ‘Le Chemin Blanc’ 2025
  • Gérard Boulay Chavignol Sancerre
  • Francois Cotat ‘Cul de Beaujeu’
  • Gérard Boulay ‘Clos de Beaujeu’
  • Gérard Boulay Sancerre Les Monts Damnes

“The 2024 ‘Le Tournebride’ Sancerre from Vincent Gaudry has been a recent standout. Vincent is legendary for securing the first biodynamic certification in Sancerre as well as intentionally blending grapes from all three of Sancerre’s primary soil types which is a nod to Parisian bistro traditions. The overall mouthfeel is great and its minerality was gentler than we’ve found with other Sancerres. And at around $50 a bottle, it holds up beautifully to a variety of food pairings from our roasted chicken to our croquettes du jour.” —Jennie Kelley, owner, Fond, Dallas

“I like Lucien Crochet, specifically the 2024 Lucien Crochet Sancerre ‘La Croix du Roy.’ It is a really classic representation but leans more herbal and basil rather than green pepper, which makes it versatile with food. Crisp and citrusy — perfect for summer!” —Charlotte Mirzoeff, general manager and beverage director, Arthur, Brooklyn

“When it comes to sheer consumption, I don’t know if there’s a Sancerre I’ve personally enjoyed or poured for guests more than Domaine Vacheron’s Guigne-Chèvres Sancerre Blanc. Produced from the estate’s famed biodynamically farmed Guigne-Chèvres vineyard, this is a wine that remains laser-focused and expressive, vintage after vintage. It’s always a staple in my home collection. The vineyard’s limestone-rich soils impart an unmistakable minerality that gives the wine an energy that dances across the palate, both playful and powerful. Whether enjoyed fresh in its youth or with a few years of bottle age, Guigne-Chèvres never fails to captivate the entire table and remind both new wine lovers and longtime aficionados that the concept of terroir is alive and well. It’s one of those rare white wines that consistently wins over even the most devoted red wine drinkers.” —Marcie Gsteiger-Cox, wine and service director, Passage, Whidbey Island, Wash.

“Vincent Gaudry has farmed biodynamically since the late ’90s, before the practice was embraced in the region. His wines are textural and precise without being scary expensive. They’re saltier and deeper than your average Sancerre. ‘Le Tournebride’ offers the most easygoing value, but go with ‘Mélodie de Vieilles Vignes’ for something more powerful.” —Grace Rogers, sommelier, Stars, New York City

“For me, Sancerre is a bit of a ‘chef’s night off’ thing, tucked in the back of my wine fridge whenever the need to chill out big time hits. But recently I’ve been really enjoying keeping the wines of Domaine B. Millet on hand with their delicious core of minerality and levity that bucks the flabby Savvy B allegations. Domaine B. Millet Sancerre ‘Le Chemin Blanc’ 2025 is a true standout.” —Alexya Brown, content strategy, Domestique Wine and founder, Vino Verité, Washington, D.C.

“Gérard Boulay, located in the Chavignol sub-zone, is a producer I always look to for cost-to-value Sancerre. Chavignol is the 90210 of Sancerre, containing some of the most coveted single vineyards there. Boulay’s style is very regal and to me, it leans vibrant and textured on the palate, yet remains very taut. You get the herbaceousness and zestiness associated with Sauvignon Blanc, but there is a more mineral, powdery, stony mouthfeel that’s very unique and special.” —Nader Asgari-Tari, director of wine, BCB3 Hospitality, Boston

“Sauvignon Blanc is kind of my comfort grape and I love to see it transmute into all of its various forms. And to me, Sancerre is another one of its gorgeous identities. Francois Cotat ‘Cul de Beaujeu’ offers this tense, generous expression, that I feel blows the door off the style in a freaky, expectation-defying way.” —Hannah Carroll, beverage director, Shy Bird, Boston

“To find Sancerres that are worth the money, I always avoid those in the $30 to $45 range, as those tend to be bottles that were $25 in 2020 and haven’t necessarily gained in quality but certainly have in price. I’d actually pick something higher end like Gerard Boulay’s ‘Clos de Beaujeu.’ It’s a bolder style from some of the best vineyard sites in the region that pairs really well with food. His ‘Monts Damnes,’ while more expensive, is my absolute favorite Sancerre — just incredibly balanced and a really great representation of the region from super steep slopes.” —Savannah Johnson, general manager, Rude Mouth, Brooklyn

Opening a restaurant in New York is difficult, even when the people behind it come from one of the best restaurants in the world. When Cedric Nicaise and chef Andy Quinn set out to open The Noortwyck, they wanted to create a true West Village neighborhood restaurant — something very different from Eleven Madison Park, the three-Michelin-starred restaurant where both previously worked. While building The Noortwyck has not been easy, it created the opportunity to open Oriana, their more approachable take on fine dining that’s already attracting attention and acclaim.

On this episode of “The Buildout,” Cedric joins Adam to discuss learning from mistakes, the importance of service and hospitality, and what restaurant critics get right — and wrong — about the dining experience.

title: 7 of the Best Chardonnays From France’s Beaujolais, a Region Famous for Reds
summary:
While the Beaujolais region of France, just south of Burgundy, is famous for its red wines made from the Gamay variety, did you know that it grows small amounts of Chardonnay as well? It turns out that Beaujolais Blanc is one of the best-kept secrets of the broader Burgundy region and is gaining more recognition.

The article 7 of the Best Chardonnays From France’s Beaujolais, a Region Famous for Reds appeared first on VinePair.
content:
While the Beaujolais region of France, just south of Burgundy, is famous for its red wines made from the Gamay variety, did you know that it grows small amounts of Chardonnay as well?

It turns out that Beaujolais Blanc is one of the best-kept secrets of the broader Burgundy region and is gaining more recognition. (Beaujolais is technically part of Burgundy, though the soils and the red wines — Gamay versus Pinot Noir — are distinct, which is why most people in the wine world consider them separate regions.)

The white wines have always intrigued me, and they are quite similar to Burgundian Chardonnays, though perhaps more on the fruity side and made either with or without oak aging. When wood is used, it tends to accent rather than dominate.

Perhaps the biggest difference is the price: While good white Burgundies, even those from the more humble Mâcon subregion in the south, can cost $30, $40, $50, and more, most Beaujolais Blancs are in the more comfortable $20 to $30 range. And well worth it.

Field Blend Selections, the importer of the excellent Domaine Emmanuel Fellot Beaujolais Blanc, notes on its website that only 3 percent of Beaujolais’ vineyards are planted to Chardonnay, adding that “this may be the natural limit since the clay-limestone alluvial soils more suited to Chardonnay are quite rare compared to the Gamay-friendly granite soils.”

Unlike the Gamay-based wines of Beaujolais, many of which are named after the 10 crus in the north of the region, most of the white wines are produced in the south and must be labeled “Beaujolais” or “Beaujolais-Villages.”

Some of the Chardonnays are also labeled “Pierres Dorées,” which means “golden stones” and is named for an area in the south of Beaujolais where the dominant soil is yellow limestone, which is also found in Burgundy. They are considered some of the best Beaujolais Blancs.

With their modest prices and refreshing, easy-to-drink character, Beaujolais Blancs are great wines for informal, late-summer lunches and dinners and for drinking on their own.

Here are seven of the best Beaujolais Blancs:

Jean-Paul Brun Beaujolais Blanc ‘Terres Dorées’ 2024

A delicate, chalky minerality underlies this gorgeous Chardonnay and its notes of pear, honeysuckle, herb-tinged mandarin, and a hint of fennel seed. Jean-Paul Brun farms organically and the wine is aged in steel and concrete tanks. A few retailers sell it for the almost unbelievable price of around $20.

Price: $22
Buy This Wine

Emmanuel Fellot Beaujolais Blanc 2025

This is a wonderful, mineral-driven Chardonnay. Though young, its ripe fruit notes — crisp white peach, citrus, and a touch of honey — make it a pleasure to enjoy right now. There’s a touch of green apple skin, white flowers, and firm acidity on the long finish. Clean, crisp, balanced, and delicious.

Price: $24
Buy This Wine

Georges Descombes Beaujolais Blanc 2023

This wine is only available in magnums, but the double-sized bottle will be a hit when you pour it for your guests or bring it to dinner. Aged in fiberglass tanks and barrels, it’s complex and subtle — the fruit, the minerality, the acidity all in balance. Notes of ripe pear, mandarin, and touches of vanilla, white pepper, and almond combine in this notable Chardonnay.

Price: $63 (1.5 liters)
Buy This Wine

Château Pougelon Beaujolais Blanc ‘Pierres Dorées’ 2024

The aromas transport you to a peach or apricot orchard in late summer, and the ripe stone fruit notes continue in the mouth along with green apple and touches of flint and white pepper. There’s a textured minerality on the long finish. The wine is aged in stainless steel and concrete and sets a benchmark in the region for non-oaked Chardonnay.

Price: $33
Buy This Wine

Domaine de Fa Beaujolais-Villages ‘Leynes Les Magnons’ 2023

Aged in stainless steel tanks and larger used oak barrels, this wine is on the richer side, with hints of vanilla and caramel infusing notes of pear and apricot. It’s also quite herbal, adding another layer of complexity. The owners and winemakers, Maxime and Antoine Graillot, use organic and biodynamic methods and were famous in the Northern Rhône when they expanded to Beaujolais in 2013.

Price: $23
Buy This Wine

Château des Jacques Beaujolais Blanc 2024

This wine reminded me of a Mâcon-Villages Chardonnay from southern Burgundy. It’s fresh, fruity, and uncomplicated with notes of apple, white peach, and hints of honey and orange. A good-value Chardonnay from the north of Beaujolais not far from Pouilly-Fuissé in the Mâcon. Château des Jacques is part of the Louis Jadot Burgundy house.

Price: $24
Buy This Wine

Arnaud Combier ‘Blanc-Sain’ Vin de France Chardonnay 2023

It’s not clear whether this wine is from Beaujolais, Burgundy, or perhaps both. But what I do know is that it’s an excellent Chardonnay. It’s labeled as a Vin de France, which suggests a hybrid origin, and Arnaud Combier produces wines in both regions. In any event, this one drinks way above its price tag with concentrated fruit notes of ripe peach, sweet apple, pineapple, and tangerine, along with balanced acidity and touches of mint, minerals, and caramel. It’s aged in both oak barrels and stainless steel tanks. Alcohol is just 12.5 percent.

Price: $19
Buy This Wine

Next up: Red blends from the Finger Lakes

title: Why Your Espresso Martini Never Has Enough Foam (And How to Fix It)
summary:
Coffee fanatics are notoriously nit-picky. One example of their particular nature is the crema on espresso shots — that light-brown, cloudlike foam that forms over the liquid. It’s silky, pretty to look at, and gives an otherwise powerful drink a bit of aerated levity. And with the boom in popularity of the Espresso Martini, fans of the cocktail have taken on a similar pride in the methodology and presentation behind the drink: a rich, boozy coffee base, topped with a thick layer of frothy foam, and exactly three espresso beans.

The article Why Your Espresso Martini Never Has Enough Foam (And How to Fix It) appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Coffee fanatics are notoriously nit-picky. One example of their particular nature is the crema on espresso shots — that light-brown, cloudlike foam that forms over the liquid. It’s silky, pretty to look at, and gives an otherwise powerful drink a bit of aerated levity. And with the boom in popularity of the Espresso Martini, fans of the cocktail have taken on a similar pride in the methodology and presentation behind the drink: a rich, boozy coffee base, topped with a thick layer of frothy foam, and exactly three espresso beans.

This formula is what gave the cocktail its iconic look, and while it’s easy to spot a great Espresso Martini in the wild, replicating that signature layer of foam at home isn’t always as straightforward. That’s why VinePair tapped experienced bartender and Luxardo brand ambassador Laura Newman to share the secret to achieving that stunningly thick layer of froth at your home bar.

Newman admits that if she had to boil it down to just one factor, it would be the amount of ice in the shaker. “A lot of ice cubes — more than you think you need — will have a really positive effect on the amount of foam, like a measurable difference,” Newman says.

The trick is one that elite cocktail institutions leverage for aeration in their drinks: It’s common for craft cocktail bars to dedicate most of their freezer space to trays upon trays of ice cubes to make sure they have enough to shake frothy cocktails throughout a night’s service.

“You need enough ice cubes to fill a large glass in a cocktail tin,” she says. “The idea is that the more surface area you have in a shaker tin of things you’re shaking with, the more froth and texturally rich your drink will be.” The extra surface area helps reinforce the cocktail’s aeration. More ice means the liquid has more edges to ricochet against, incorporating more air along the way.

“You see the same effect with whipped cream and whipped egg whites,” she says. “You could foam egg whites using a paddle mixer attachment, but it’s not going to have the same volume as if you use the whisk attachment. The more the whisk has more points of contact, and the better it aerates.”

The biggest mistake Newman sees her friends make with at-home Espresso Martinis is shaking them with minimal ice, resulting in liquidy concoctions — not necessarily bad, but not the frothy, palate-coating goodness that some drinkers prefer. Another pitfall she notices while hosting consumer demonstrations for Luxardo’s espresso liqueur is people not shaking the cocktail for long enough.

“I see lazy and sad shakes, but I always tell consumers to shake it hard enough that the ice hits both ends of the tin,” Newman adds.

Beyond shaking for enough time with enough ice, Newman’s foremost tip for making an Espresso Martini is using cold brew or cooled-down espresso. Some cocktail purists believe the coffee component must stick to the drink’s name and refuse to use any other form of joe. To them, she cautions that the dilution caused by warm espresso will result in a lackluster cocktail.

“I’m a level two certified sommelier and am trained in blind tasting,” she says. “I can blind taste between one Espresso Martini made with hot espresso versus cold espresso, and the hot one is going to be objectively worse.”

title: NYC Insiders Club Jean’s Defines Downtown Manhattan Right Now. Can It Last?
summary:

Others hopped on the phone with promoters and begged for help getting in between vape puffs. The article NYC Insiders Club Jean’s Defines Downtown Manhattan Right Now. Can It Last? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
The line outside of Jean’s moved quickly for a Friday night. Bouncers unclipped velvet ropes for hordes of Zoomers who said they knew someone who knew someone who had a table. Others hopped on the phone with promoters and begged for help getting in between vape puffs. Protein-maxxing bros and girls in short skirts stepped out of black Cadillacs and, without turning their heads, marched past the glass doors. All the while, the line kept moving.

Surely, you’ve heard of Jean’s. You might’ve seen someone post from the upstairs bistro or downstairs club. Maybe you’ve scrolled past the jumbo chocolate chip cookies or the branded gua sha that Jean’s sent to its most loyal — and most followed — regulars.

Jean’s is a restaurant with a club — some might call it a clubstaurant — on Lafayette Street owned by Max Chodorow, nepo baby to Jeffrey Chodorow, the famed restaurateur behind institutions like China Grill. Ashwin Deshmukh, a “nightclub impresario” involved in buzzy New York City spots like vegetarian haunt Superiority Burger, is also a partner.

Since opening in 2023, Jean’s has established itself as the glitziest hangout for NYC’s cool crowd: Influencers, designers, DJs, writers, and other well-connected partiers. Though snagging a reservation to eat gluten-free mozzarella rings upstairs might be easy, getting into the club below — as I came to find out that Friday evening — is either a shot in the dark or a cake walk. It just depends on who you are, who you know, or what you look like.

When it was our turn to get sized up by the bouncer at around 11 p.m., we were forced to admit that no, we didn’t have a reservation, and no, we weren’t on the guest list.

“I can do a bar tab for $600 for the three of you,” she offered us while twiddling a metal number ticker in her hand. The bouncer was choosy. That’s fine. That is her job and this is mine.

Jean’s has maintained its grip on the minds of NYC’s cool, current partygoers for roughly three years now — an impressive feat for a spot geared toward a generation that’s always ready to hop to the next hot spot.

Hangouts for the glitterati have always been exclusive. Some are a flash in the pan, whereas others — say Studio 54 — become longstanding institutions. When the demand is getting in and the supply is exclusivity, as is the case at Jean’s, the model has proven to work. The question that remains, then, is whether it can or will join the ranks of such historic spots.

Farm-to-Table-to-Bottle-Service

Early coverage on its opening billed Jean’s as a “farm-to-table bistro” where “produce is upfront.” Those descriptors aren’t untrue: Jean’s sources its produce from Chodorow’s farm in Pennsylvania, and dishes like steak au poivre and agnolotti with courgettes are on the menu.

“The food is honestly better than it needs to be,” says J Lee, food critic for Feed Me, a popular Substack for NYC’s food and finance in-crowd, who hosted his wedding ceremony, dinner, and reception across the two floors of Jean’s last year. “I remember I was quite impressed with it the first time I went. It’s all fun food that nobody can really be mad at.”

Now, though, most of its buzz has pivoted downstairs. Many in my orbit of 20-somethings were well aware of the dance club Jean’s, but ignorant of its associated restaurant. How did a hotly anticipated restaurant that made its rounds in NYC’s elite food media publications become almost entirely eclipsed by a downstairs club? What draws Brooklynites to pass over the clubs in Bushwick in exchange for hopping on the L train and taking a chance on getting turned away at the door?

Like the origin story for many of NYC’s buzziest clubs, Jean’s found its way with cool kids via luxury brands and socialite-filled parties. Jimmy Choo and Barbour have hosted branded parties, inviting downtown icons of yore and viral scenesters today — Chloë Sevigny, Martha Stewart, and Emily Ratajkowski, among others — to its club space. On a given weekend night, you might see below-14th Street media personalities like Instagram-popular writer and DJ Alex Delany, Feed Me’s founder Emily Sundberg, and Gutes Guterman, publisher of Byline and The Drunken Canal.

“We felt part of the upper echelon of the downtown scene. The door is hard as hell, but once you get past it, everyone’s family.”

Exclusivity at Jean’s is unabashed. “The line is just for you to wait to talk to us,” the bouncer said after determining us unworthy of entry. Fair play. There’s also an entire page on Resy’s website with former general manager Kahiem Rivera walking the Jean’s-dreamers through the savoir-faire of gaining entry. One suggested workaround is to book a table in the restaurant and inquire the waitstaff about going downstairs. Rivera also advises those without a reservation to “come with a small group, look your best, and try your luck at the door.”

One 20-something who once dined and danced at Jean’s — and requested anonymity for this piece — said its insiders club reputation is the very reason it’s so enticing. If you’ve been, you’ve been.

“It’s a highly coveted reservation and spot,” they said. “We felt part of the upper echelon of the downtown scene. The door is hard as hell, but once you get past it, everyone’s family.”

Jean’s plays into its intrigue with deft marketing stunts and an Instagram following of in-the-know frequenters and curious hopefuls. The clubstaurant sends a blood-red gua sha branded with “Jean’s” in the signature script to its roster of popular regulars, who post and boast the skincare tool.

“The craziest part is they make you want this gua sha so bad,” the 20-something said, who pushed their own company to host an event at Jean’s for yet another chance of getting in. “If you have the gua sha, then you join the elite community.”

Then again, Jean’s isn’t for everyone. “There’s not enough aura here,” one man with salt-and-pepper hair said over the phone as he dipped off the line.

Can ‘Club’ Stand for ‘Cultural Hub?’

In many ways, Jean’s is on track to becoming an institution: It welcomes of-the-moment influencers, it demands a $600 cover from three people looking to party, and it bought a historic Hamptons restaurant for $4.5 million with plans of opening a new outpost out east next summer.

“Jean’s wanted to be more than just a popping club on the weekends,” Lee says. “It wanted to be a cultural meeting place in New York City in a way that feels old-school, that feels like an older generation of New York.”

That nexus of culture harkens back to a time when the media, publishing, and fashion elite ruled the NYC scene. And it’s not just modern media: The old glossies of Condé Nast are also attracted to Jean’s. The New Yorker celebrated its centennial at Jean’s last year, and earlier this year, Vogue’s Anna Wintour hosted Will Welch’s farewell party as he stepped down as global editorial director at GQ.

Lee feels a rush of familiarity and of all-things culture each time he steps in. He bumps into fellow tastemakers on any given visit. “Maybe it’s a writer, maybe an artist, or a fashion designer, but they do a good job of being very hospitable to the people that they think are cultural movers and shakers in the city,” he says.

Can Radical Exclusivity Bide Time?

It appears that, so far, the radically exclusive ethos at Jean’s has not stymied its allure, as evidenced by the near guarantee that city kids will assemble on Lafayette Street each Friday and Saturday night. That guarantee may not last for years to come — in NYC, it’s almost too easy for a spot to lose its “cool” factor. The latest victim of this phenomenon might just be cocktail bar Kind Regards, a previous hot spot in the Lower East Side that shuttered earlier this month.

Jean’s did not respond to VinePair’s multiple requests for comment, nor did former and current employees.

“As much as it has this reputation of being an exclusive, hard-to-get-into club on Friday and Saturday nights, they do a good job of like keeping their finger on the pulse with things that they actually f*ck with,” Lee says. “They do a good job of being hospitable and amenable to like organizations and to people that they think are cool.”

Is hospitality actually hospitality when Jean’s cherry picks certain patrons to be hospitable to? If, for the majority, exclusivity is the sole product, how much staying power can it retain?

“I’m scared to try and get in when I’m not associated with a brand,” the 20-something said. “I’m lucky to have done what I’ve done there. I don’t know if I’ll ever get it again.”

title: 7 Grape Varieties to Try if You Love Pinot Noir
summary:
Pinot Noir is the soufflé of red grapes: notoriously finicky to cultivate, yet highly coveted and utterly sublime in the right hands. content:
Pinot Noir is the soufflé of red grapes: notoriously finicky to cultivate, yet highly coveted and utterly sublime in the right hands. Known for bright acidity and silky tannins, the thin-skinned grape often delivers layers of red fruit, florals, earth, herbs, and spice. That complexity has earned Pinot Noir a fiercely devoted following, with the wines of Burgundy, its historic stronghold, among the most prized in the world.

But Pinot Noir has also found a home in other cool-climate regions around the globe, like Oregon’s Willamette Valley, California’s Central Coast, and Germany, where it’s called Spätburgunder. It’s even one of the principal grapes used to make Champagne — just one example of how many forms Pinot can take.

“Pinot Noir is a difficult grape to put in a box,” says Tynan Pierce, wine director of Yes Society. “It can take on so many different personalities depending on where it’s grown and how it’s made,” he says, pointing to a richer, more structured Pinot Noir from the Sonoma Coast versus a more delicate, classic expression from Burgundy. So before looking for an alternative, it’s important to consider what you love about Pinot in the first place.

Is it the aromatic complexity? The juicy red fruit? Or maybe the grape’s freshness, acidity, or food-friendliness? While no grape is a perfect stand-in, plenty share some of the same qualities that keep its devotees heading straight to the Pinot aisle at the wine shop. For those ready to branch out, here are seven grape varieties to try next, moving from those with plenty of similarities to less expected alternatives.

Gamay

Arguably the closest alternative on the list, Gamay is a natural cross between Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc, and the family resemblance shows up in its light-to-medium body, lively acidity, low tannins, and punchy red fruit. For a classic style, look for Beaujolais, where Gamay reigns after being famously banished from neighboring Burgundy in the 14th century. As a producer of both Pinot Noir and Gamay, Story of Soil winemaker Jessica Gasca says Gamay “tends to be a little more playful and fruit-forward, but with an added savory component.” Try Gasca’s Martian Vineyard Gamay Noir or, for classic Beaujolais, she recommends producers like Daniel Bouland and Domaine Lapierre.

Cinsault

If Pinot’s soft tannins and juicy fruit are your vibe, it’s time to give Cinsault a try. There’s also a good chance you’ve tasted it before and just don’t know it. Historically used in blends throughout the Rhône and Provence, Cinsault produces delicate tannins with ripe cherry and strawberry notes, helping soften and lift more powerful varieties like Grenache, Syrah, and Mourvèdre. Ali Schmidt, wine director at Emmer & Rye Hospitality, likens it to a “warm-weather Pinot”: While both are thin-skinned, Cinsault thrives in hot climates where Pinot struggles. To sample it yourself, Schmidt suggests Craven Cinsault from Stellenbosch or William Chris’ Lost Draw Cinsault from the Texas High Plains.

Frappato

Think of Frappato as Pinot Noir with a Mediterranean flair. Native to Sicily, it’s another grape historically blended with the more boisterous Nero d’Avola, but don’t underestimate its beauty as a single-varietal wine. Bottled solo, Frappato produces light, silky reds that are anything but simple. Chris Dillman, director of wine at Littleton’s Market in Columbus, Ohio, loves Frappato for its “glossy ripe red fruit and rounded, mouth-filling character,” but notes that wood spice, olive, and potpourri aromas show its Mediterranean origins. Dillman recommends seeking out Sicilian producers Occhipinti or COS.

Sangiovese

Ever ordered a Tuscan red at an Italian restaurant? Chances are, you’ve already had Sangiovese, the region’s signature red grape. For Pinot fans, expect a similar combination of red fruit, medium body, and savory character, though Sangiovese typically brings a touch more acidity and tannin to the table. “If you’re drawn to the elegant, earthy aromas of Pinot Noir,” says Lucy Grundhauser, sommelier at Lei Wine Bar in New York City, “consider the rustically herbaceous nose of Sangiovese — it’s a slightly more adventurous counterpart while still maintaining similar Old World sensibilities.” And while some Pinots set you back a pretty penny, Sangiovese can deliver at nearly any price point. Grundhauser recommends Fonterenza Rosso di Montalcino or Caparsa ‘Caparsino’ Chianti Classico Riserva.

Grenache

Don’t write off Grenache as only a big, jammy red. Like Pinot, it has range. Common in southern Rhône blends and known as Garnacha in Spain, Grenache can swing from ripe and fruit-forward to elegant and savory. While it lacks Pinot’s hallmark acidity, Ben Kaehler, general manager of The Walls Vineyards in Walla Walla, Wash., says it offers the same freshness and lift, with cherry and raspberry alongside floral, herbal, and savory characteristics. Kaehler recommends PÁŠXA Grenache from Washington’s Rocks District for a restrained, earthy style that showcases the grape’s elegant side.

País

Long seen as a humble, everyday wine, País deserves a second look from Pinot drinkers drawn to lively, rustic reds with wild strawberry, cherry, and an earthy character. The grape also goes by many names — Mission in California and Criolla Chica in Argentina — but País has a centuries-long history in Chile, where remarkably old, ungrafted vines survive today. For a taste of País at its wildest, try J. Bouchon País Salvaje, made from 100-plus-year-old vines that grow wild among the trees in Chile’s Maule Valley.

Mencía

For a little bit of everything Pinot lovers crave, look to Mencía. Native to northwestern Spain, where it’s best known in Bierzo, Ribeira Sacra, and Valdeorras, expect something a little more savory and peppery than Pinot, with tart cherry, red currant, and bright acidity. Tess Housholder, lead sommelier at Appellation Healdsburg, calls the Spanish variety the “Goldilocks grape” for its triple-threat combo of red fruit, earthiness, and spice. For your first bottle, start with Mencía from Bierzo or Ribeira Sacra.

title: The VinePair Podcast: You Can Be Exclusive Without Being Jerks
summary:
Today on the “VinePair Podcast,” Adam, Joanna, and Zach discuss a recent occurrence from filming The Wait: A trendy NYC restaurant told people to come back at 11 p.m. for dinner and, when they did come back, informed them that the kitchen was closed. Was this just a random bit of bad hospitality, or was it an ill-founded attempt to make this restaurant feel more exclusive and pretentious? To whom does that kind of pretension appeal, anyway?

title: Tilray to Cease Production at Terrapin Beer Co.’s Georgia Brewery
summary:
Tilray Brands will cease brewing at Terrapin Beer Co.’s 100,000 sq. ft. facility in Athen’s, Ga. The brand will shift production to other plants within its network starting Sept. 25, though the site’s taproom and warehouse will remain in operation, according to a report from The Red & Black. The move is part of a larger consolidation plan for Tilray Brands, a Canada-based producer of cannabis and beverage goods, in the aim of increasing efficiency across its breweries.

content:
Tilray Brands will cease brewing at Terrapin Beer Co.’s 100,000 sq. ft. facility in Athen’s, Ga. The brand will shift production to other plants within its network starting Sept. 25, though the site’s taproom and warehouse will remain in operation, according to a report from The Red & Black.

The move is part of a larger consolidation plan for Tilray Brands, a Canada-based producer of cannabis and beverage goods, in the aim of increasing efficiency across its breweries. In a 10-K filing from July 28, Tilray looped Terrapin, along with its other beer brands like Hop Valley, Redhook, and Revolver, into a cost-cutting initiative called Project 420.

Tilray disclosed it spent $6.8 million in Project 420 restructuring costs in fiscal year 2026, which ended May 31. The company anticipates the closures, consolidations, and other restructurings will be largely completed by the end of fiscal 2027.

While many players in the craft industry, both big and small, have struggled or shuttered over the past few years, Tilray has notably invested big in the industry. The company scooped up eight brands from Anheuser-Busch InBev in 2023 and four brands from Molson Coors, including Terrapin, in 2024. Earlier this year, Tilray bought BrewDog for $44 million and inked a deal with the Carlsberg Group to produce, market, and sell the Danish beer in the U.S.

The beverage business remains “one of Tilray’s most important growth engines,” CEO Irwin Simon said in an earnings call. And Simon suggests the company is still in the “early stages of unlocking full potential of this business.” In fiscal year 2026, Tilray earned $254 million in beverage net revenue, a jump from the previous fiscal year’s $240.6 million net revenue.

content:
By now most people know there are geographically-protected wines — that whole “Actually, it’s only Champagne if it comes from” meme. Less discussed, however, are Europe’s geographically-protected spirits. There are the obvious ones, always capitalized, like Scotch, Cognac, Armagnac, and Calvados. But there is also a geographically-protected gin that is a bit more obscure.

Spain’s Gin de Mahón.

Produced since 1750 on the tiny island of Menorca, one of the Balearic Islands located in the Mediterranean Sea, roughly 130 due east of the mainlaid, it is said that the occupying British Royal Navy was what initially spurred locals to produce it. But Menorca was a grape-growing island — specifically Parellada grapes used for Cava — making for an atypical base distillate for gin.

The family Destilerías Xoriguer has been distilling what is now known as Mahón gin since 1945, supposedly based on the original 18th century recipe. (While most cocktail menus in the U.S. will simply list the Xoriguer product as “Mahón Gin” or “Gin de Mahón,” it should be noted there is a smaller craft distiller, Licores Biniarbolla, also producing gins on the island.) Xoriguer distills on wood-fired pot stills over 250 years old using juniper sourced from the Pyrenees — then aged near the Mahón harbor for two years — along with other undisclosed botanicals before being matured in American oak then bottled in its unique emerald green, handled caneca jug.

While long a source of pride on the island, Mahón Gin has remained mostly obscure in the United States until recently, where a trend of Spanish-style cocktails has led to its rise in New York and beyond.

Simple and Complex

At Mirador, an Andalucían-inspired tapas café in Kingston, the Martini Mirador has been served with Mahón since the spot first opened in early 2024. The gin is paired with an extra dry sherry-based vermouth, fino sherry, olive brine, and a garnish of a fino sherry gelatin cubito served as a pintxo with a Gordal olive placed next to it.

“We chose Mahón gin for three reasons: first and foremost because of its purity; second because it’s grape-based which aligns with our love of Spanish wine; and third because the roundness and purity pair very nicely with a slightly more robust fino sherry,” says Mirador’s owner Nick Africano. “Everything in the Martini is grape-based (apart from the olive).”

Africano considers Mahón a gin that is somehow both simple and complex, one that can star in a gin- and juniper-forward Martini yet can also allow sherry and vermouth to have their own voices as there are not a slew of botanicals in the gin fighting for dominance. In fact, it seems many bars love the interplay between Mahón and sherry. There is a clear minerality, but a warmth and woodiness from the slight barrel-aging that you just don’t see in more standard London dry gins.

(For these reasons and more, it recently tied for 1st as our top overall scoring gin on VinePair’s Best Gins for 2026.)

This unique and distinct flavor profile almost demands a sort of Martini template: Mahón + sherry + vermouth + salty garnish.

At Deux Chats, “Le bar préféré de Williamsburg: Martinis & Oysters” according to their motto, the house Deux Chats Martini is served with Mahón Gin alongside manzanilla sherry, dry vermouth, and celery brine. Bodega Nights in Bushwick makes their Martini with Mahón, fino sherry, Tximista blanco vermouth, and a Gilda garnish. While Rolo’s Martini Spanish pairs Mahón with sherry, Atxa blanco vermouth, olive brine, and pepper.

This template is taken to extremes at buzzy and theatrical West Village restaurant Wild Cherry. There, diners are encouraged to end their meal with a shot of chilled Mahón poured into a conch shell they’ve just eaten chilled scungilli braised in a court bouillon broth from. This becomes a sort of oceanic ice luge shooter.

“We chose Mahón gin for three reasons: first and foremost because of its purity; second because it’s grape-based which aligns with our love of Spanish wine; and third because the roundness and purity pair very nicely with a slightly more robust fino sherry.”

Initially, head bartender Karlos Hernandez had figured the maritime brine and broth of the conch might pair best with a smoky, vegetal mezcal — but that didn’t quite work. His thought then moved toward Mahón, recalling how it is made with juniper aged for a couple of years in open crates by the salty ocean air.

“In my head, I knew that if stirred with a touch of Maldon salt, the oils and bitter botanicals in the gin would complement the court bouillon’s earthy and sweet whelk flavor, and so we gave it a go,” says Hernandez. “The natural ocean salinity of the dish paired very well with the Mahón, a complementary flavor but also a perfect texture and weight to mix with the court bouillon.”

An Ointment That Spread

But Mahón need not be elevated and used in baroque cocktails necessarily either.

The quintessential Menorcan way to drink its local gin is in a pomada (“ointment”), a blend of the spirit and lemonade or lemon soda. It’s the ideal summer drink, ladled from a punch bowl or batched and pulled from the freezer to serve to friends and neighbors during the fiesta season.

And, no surprise, that is how it is served (sorta) at José Andres Mercado Little Spain in Manhattan’s Hudson Yards. In the food hall’s Txula Steak there is a Pomada Gin Mule built of Mahón Gin lemon, mint, Fever-Tree ginger beer, Fever-Tree club soda, and bergamot oil. Mahón is also a house favorite — recommended by Andres no less! — in their Spanish Gin-Tonic.

Similarly, the Boqueria mini-chain of Spanish tapas restaurants throughout New York include Mahón in their signature Gin Tonic, which currently comes with Lillet Rosé and rhubarb bitters as well. As does El Quijote at the Chelsea Hotel, which uses Mahón in their Quijote G+T alongside pear, aloe, and celery. While Vern’s in Rochester deploys Mahón in their Spanish G + T with an herb bouquet and citrus.

“Spanish-style cocktails are having a moment in the U.S. right now because of how deeply flavorful and diverse the products are,” says Africano. “From low ABV spritzes to spirit forward Martinis, the products of Spain cover all the bases. Many of the cocktails also have culturally significant rituals, and drinking those cocktails here in the U.S. transports us to a place and to a certain kind of experience.”

However, a big reason Mahón has surely exploded in New York isn’t purely flavor- or trend-based. PM Spirits, that so-called “provider of geeky spirits,” has been the brand’s New York and New York only importer since 2014.

As of earlier this summer, though, PM Spirits has taken over as national importer. Meaning, Mahón mania is soon to spread across the country.
